parts.required:
Provide an analysis of the following areas of the bank's performance from 2018 to 2022 based on the information in the appendices (including your calculations above).

a. The bank's profitability
parts.memo:
Lecturer's answer. NIM has been declining steadily over time. There was a brief bounce-back in 2021 as the effects of the pandemic were reversed but 2022 performance is in line with that last seen in 2020 during the initial lockdown problems. The issue in the most recent period has been declining NII brought about by interest expense increasing more than interest income. This would seem to indicate that the spread between the two has shrunk in the most recent period.

ROA is also declining steadily over time and is now at its lowest level in 5 years (apart from the obvious issues in 2020 thanks to lockdown). This is a consequence of both profit margin and asset utilization declining. This is in line with the shrinking spread between interest income and expense coupled with increasing assets.

Coupled with all of the above, the leverage has also declined over time, quite significantly. While this lowers the bank's risk, it also means that their ROE is lower as a result. Clearly, all the performance metrics for the bank have declined over time and are concerning.

parts.required:
Provide an analysis of the following areas of the bank's performance from 2018 to 2022 based on the information in the appendices (including your calculations above).

b. The bank's cost efficiencies
parts.memo:
Lecturer's answer. The bank's cost-to-income ratio has been quite consistent over the past few years at roughly 58%. This is higher than the ideal ratio of 50% but not so high as to be concerning. If this was a South African bank, for example, this would be roughly on par with what is expected. The bank's operating expenses have actually decreased in the most recent period but the declining profits mean the measure has worsened overall.

The JAWS ratio of the bank has generally been positive which shows that income is growing faster than expenses. The exception was 2020 during lockdown, which makes sense. Having said that, the JAWS ratio has consistently been only slightly positive showing that income hasn't been growing significantly faster than expenses and this might be a cause for concern for the bank.

parts.required:
Provide an analysis of the following areas of the bank's performance from 2018 to 2022 based on the information in the appendices (including your calculations above).

c. The bank's risk
parts.memo:
Lecturer's answer. The credit loss ratio of the bank has consistently been in the ideal band of 1-3%, even during 2020. This speaks to the quality of the bank's loan book. Having said that, there might be a question of whether the bank is not being overly conservative in its lending as it may be able to improve its margins by lending out to slightly higher risk clients at higher rates.

The loan-to-deposit ratio of the bank has also consistently been in the ideal band of 80% to 90%. This suggests the bank is deriving the bulk of its earnings from loans with only a small portion of its deposit funds invested in other assets.

Finally, the bank's leverage as indicated earlier is quite low with quite a big decline in the most recent period. While this is positive from a risk perspective, it does mean that the bank is missing out on the benefits of leverage at a time when its performance could use improvement.

Supplement (from the compiled Q&A, not the lecturer's): the memo slip: the credit loss ratio was in fact below 1% in every year except 2020 (1,6%): 0,5%-0,9%. The conclusion (good loan quality) is unchanged.

parts.required:
Assume you had to conduct a valuation of Willow Bank.

a. Briefly discuss the reasons a free cash flow valuation would not be appropriate.
parts.memo:
Lecturer's answer. Any of the points from the slides would be appropriate here - issues around debt being hard to define for a bank, working capital not really having any meaning, capex not being a driver of growth, depreciation not being significant, etc.

Supplement (from the compiled Q&A, not the lecturer's): debt is hard to define for a bank (treating deposits as debt would overstate free cash flow); interest is part of operations, so operating and financing cash flows cannot be separated; working capital has no real meaning because almost all of the balance sheet is current; capex is not the driver of growth and depreciation is insignificant; high leverage; regulatory capital constraints on growth.

parts.required:
Assume you had to conduct a valuation of Willow Bank.

b. If you had the option of valuing the bank using a relative valuation (multiples) method approach, would you prefer to use the price-to-book ratio or price-to-earnings ratio as your multiple? Why?
parts.memo: Lecturer's answer. Price-to-book would be preferred as bank's mark to market daily and there is therefore a strong link between the bank's market price and its book value of equity. The issue with using PE ratio is that banks are able to smooth their earnings using their credit impairments. This leaves PE ratio open to manipulation and makes it harder to use as a relative valuation measure.

questions.title: Question 2 — Working capital
questions.scenario:
You have been provided the following financial data about a firm:

Credit Sales – R15000
Cost of Sales – R12000
Average Accounts Receivable – R1800
Average Accounts Payable – R1200
Beginning Inventory Balance – R1650
Ending Inventory Balance – R1400

parts.required: Calculate the operating cycle of the firm.
parts.memo:
Lecturer's answer. Operating cycle = No. of days of inventory + No. of days of receivables.

Average Inventory = (1,650 + 1,400) / 2 = 1,525

No. of days of inventory = 1,525 / (12,000 / 365) = 46.37 days [3 marks]

No. of days of receivables = 1,800 / (15,000 / 365) = 43.8 days [2 marks]

Therefore, Operating cycle = 46.37 days + 43.8 days = 90.17 days [1 mark]

Supplement (from the compiled Q&A, not the lecturer's): 1 525 x 365 / 12 000 is 46,39 days, so the memo's 46,37 is a small rounding slip; the operating cycle is about 90,2 days. Payables (R1 200) are not used: they belong to the cash conversion cycle, not the operating cycle.

parts.required: How could the firm improve its operating cycle?
parts.memo:
Lecturer's answer. Anything here that would improve either DSO or DIO. Note that DPO is not appropriate given that it is not part of the operating cycle calculation.

Supplement (from the compiled Q&A, not the lecturer's): to cut DIO: just-in-time or consignment stock, better forecasting, removing slow-moving lines. To cut DSO: tighter credit terms, early-payment discounts, prompt invoicing and collection, factoring.
